This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

As of December 11, 2024, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), report [58 confirmed human cases of H5 avian influenza](https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary/index.html) in the United States. So far 56 of these cases have been connected to exposure from cattle or poultry, though the exposure source of two of these cases is unknown.

The spread of H5 avian influenza among birds and cattle and its spread to humans has [raised concerns](https://www.today.com/health/disease/bird-flu-pandemic-rcna183174) that it could turn into another pandemic. > * Person-to-person spread: None
> * Current public health risk: Low

In the United States, declarations of a [public health emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health_emergency_(United_States)) (PHE) can allow the government to [take a number of emergency preparedness and response actions](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/Pages/phe-qa.aspx). [According to the US Department of Health and Human Services](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/pages/default.aspx) (HHS):

>The Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) may, under section 319 of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act determine that: a) a disease or disorder presents a public health emergency; or b) that a public health emergency, including significant outbreaks of infectious disease or bioterrorist attacks, otherwise exists. 

The HHS maintains [a page of all prior PHE declarations](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/pages/default.aspx) since August of 2005, including for the four disease outbreaks designated in that period of [H1N1](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/Pages/h1n1-26Apr2009.aspx), [Zika](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/Pages/zika-pr.aspx), [COVID-19](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/Pages/2019-nCoV.aspx), and [Mpox](https://aspr.hhs.gov/legal/PHE/Pages/monkeypox-4Aug22.aspx), each of which was renewed at least once.

* The state or territory designated for the public health emergency is immaterial, any declaration will count.

**H5N1 Avian Influenza: How Dangerous Is It? Risks to Humans, Animals, and the Pandemic Threat**
The highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza virus continues to spread across wild bird populations in Europe, particularly among cranes and waterfowl such as ducks and geese, according to the Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut (FLI). In Germany and Europe, 15 outbreaks have been reported since September 1, 2025, in poultry farms, leading to the culling of thousands of birds—most notably over 35,000 chickens in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Experts rate the risk of H5N1 entering poultry holdings as very high, with transmission occurring via contact with wild birds, their droppings, or contaminated clothing and equipment. Zoo and wildlife park birds are also at risk. While H5N1 has infected 992 humans globally—mainly in Asia, Turkey, Spain, the UK, and the US—symptoms in humans are typically mild due to the virus’s limited ability to bind to human cell receptors. However, a single mutation, such as Q226L, could significantly enhance its human receptor-binding capacity. The virus remains non-transmissible between humans and requires further mutations to become a human pandemic threat. A key concern is the potential for genetic reassortment if a human is co-infected with H5N1 and seasonal influenza, as seen in the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. In the US, H5N1 outbreaks in dairy cows have been reported since 2024, with viral particles detected in raw milk (up to 20% of supermarket samples tested positive), though these cases were primarily caused by a less pathogenic variant. The FLI assesses the risk to cattle and raw milk contamination in Europe as very low, citing no import of raw milk or live cattle from the US to Germany and the processing of imported dairy products that renders viral infectivity unlikely. A single infected sheep in England was likely exposed via contaminated milking equipment on a farm with infected poultry.

**Warnings Over Avian Influenza Reaching Australian Territories: Scientists Raise Alarm, Government Assures Preparedness**
Scientists have detected potential signs of bird flu in elephant seals on Heard Island, an Australian external territory, with field observations aligning with avian influenza symptoms, though confirmation is pending. Laboratory testing of samples is scheduled for November. While no unusual bird deaths have been reported among penguins or other marine birds, the Australian Department of Agriculture describes the situation as a 'warning sign' requiring serious preparedness for a possible outbreak. The government has allocated over AUD 100 million for surveillance, response planning, and additional funding for environmental groups monitoring wildlife. Researcher Jane Younger from the University of Tasmania warned that a potential outbreak on Heard Island could be catastrophic for regional wildlife and Australia, noting the virus has spread rapidly across the Southern Ocean in the past six months, with Macquarie Island and mainland Australia as potential next targets. She cited up to 90% chick mortality in some affected areas globally and warned marine birds would be among the first casualties. Although human infections with H5N1 are rare, the World Health Organization reported dozens of cases in the past two years, mostly among poultry workers, including one death in the U.S. Scientists caution that genetic mutations allowing the virus to jump from birds to cattle could increase the risk of a human-transmissible pandemic. Senanayake stated that the virus’s ability to jump to cattle was unexpected and must be closely monitored, as avian flu could be the seed of the next global pandemic. Australia remains the only continent without a confirmed H5N1 outbreak, but its geographic location and migratory bird routes make it highly vulnerable. While the government expresses confidence in rapid response capabilities, scientists stress that prevention hinges on continuous monitoring and public awareness.
